chapters.title: Rupert Comes Clean
chapters.text:
Rupert Ashby found Hattie on Wednesday morning at the bakery counter, his cap twisted in both hands like a wet dishrag. Biscuit took one look at him from the windowsill and turned his orange back. "I lied to you," Rupert said. "About the morning of the bake-off. I wasn't fixing the furnace at the inn. I was in Bangor, sitting across a desk from a bank officer."

Hattie set down a tray of cinnamon buns and reached for her green notebook. "Why on earth keep that a secret?" Rupert's ears went pink. "Because the whole village would know by lunchtime that the Gull's Rest is drowning in debt. I was begging for a loan so I would never have to sell to Lionel Crane. I left before sunrise and didn't get back until the tea tent was already in an uproar."

He slid a folded card across the counter. It was an appointment card from the Coastal Savings Bank, with the date and the hour stamped in purple ink. "Mr. Pruitt will vouch for me," he said.

Hattie studied the card, then the man. He looked tired, but he did not look like someone hiding a darker secret. Still, she copied the bank's telephone number into her notebook. "Did you get the loan?" she asked gently. "Not yet," Rupert admitted. "But I would rather lose the inn honestly than keep it with a lie." Hattie wrapped him a warm cinnamon bun for the road.

chapters.title: Candlelight and Clues
chapters.text:
By Thursday evening a nor'easter came howling up the coast, rattling the bakery shutters and flinging rain at the glass. At half past seven the lights flickered twice and went out, and the whole village square sank into darkness. Biscuit gave an offended yowl from under the table.

Winnie Calloway arrived ten minutes later, dripping from her yellow slicker and carrying two thermoses of cocoa. "The bookshop is black as a coal bin," she announced. "I thought we might as well be dark together." Hattie lit every candle she owned, set them along the counter, and opened her green notebook to a fresh page.

One by one they went through the clues. The cut foxglove in the walled garden. The empty hook in the potting shed. The apron with green stains, the honey in a teacup belonging to a man who hated honey, the early train ticket, and the recipe notebook that matched Lionel's cookbook word for word. Then the contract, the unsent letter, the whiff of lavender, the muddy trowel and the small boots on the back porch.

"It's like a quilt with half the squares missing," Winnie said, licking cocoa from her lip. Winnie loved a good list almost as much as a good rumor,. "Meanwhile poor Delia gets all the blame." Hattie nodded slowly. "Every piece belongs somewhere. We just have to see the pattern." Outside, the wind moaned around the chimney, and the candle flames bent and straightened as if they were listening too.

chapters.title: Leaves in a Guidebook
chapters.text:
The morning after the storm, the Gull's Rest Inn smelled of wet wool and woodsmoke. Dottie Quill had asked Hattie to help tidy the reading room, where a leak had dripped onto the window seat and soaked a row of paperbacks. Hattie spread the damp books across the radiator.

Near the end of the shelf sat a fat guidebook called Coastal Walks of Maine, its spine cracked from years of use. When Hattie lifted it, something slid out from between the pages and landed on the rug with a soft rustle. It was a small brown envelope, the kind seed packets come in, folded over twice and held shut with a paper clip.

Hattie opened it carefully over her handkerchief. Inside were crushed dried leaves, gray-green and brittle, with a faint bitter smell that made her nose wrinkle. "Dottie, do you know who's been reading this book?" Dottie squinted at it. "Anybody. Guests borrow from these shelves all week and never sign anything out. Mr. Crane's people were in here, and Mr. Ashby, and half the committee came through for sherry on Sunday."

Hattie folded the handkerchief around the envelope and tucked it into her handbag. She wrote the title of the guidebook in her notebook, along with the page where it had been hidden, a map of the cliff path above the harbor. Something about those leaves made her uneasy, and she meant to show them to Sam before the day was out.

chapters.title: Clear Skies for Gordon
chapters.text:
Hattie walked down to the harbor office on Friday with a bag of molasses cookies. Gordon Pike was at his desk beneath a wall of tide charts, a mug of black coffee cooling by his elbow.

"I know what folks are saying," he grumbled. "That I had a reason to want Lionel quiet. Well, I did. But I never left this office the whole morning of the bake-off." He pulled a battered ledger from a drawer and flipped it open. "The radio log. Every call in and out of this harbor gets written down with the time, and I signed every single entry."

Hattie ran her finger down the column. There was Gordon's blocky handwriting at six fifteen, talking a lobster boat in through the fog. Again at seven, and seven thirty, and every quarter hour after that, right up until the siren wailed from the green. Abe Tolliver's name appeared twice, calling in from the Mary Ellen to complain about a tangled buoy line.

"Abe will tell you I answered him myself," Gordon said. Hattie smiled despite herself. Abe was the most honest grouch in Pennywhistle Harbor. She thanked Gordon, left him the rest of the cookies, and walked back up the hill with the sea wind tugging at her scarf. In her green notebook she drew a neat line through his name. It felt good to cross someone off, even if the list was still far too long.

chapters.title: Left Behind in the Tent
chapters.text:
The striped tea tent still stood on the village green, sagging a little after the storm. The committee had been too rattled to take it down, and a long trestle table near the back held crates of borrowed crockery waiting to be returned to their owners. Hattie had promised to sort it all, since half the cups came from her own cupboards.

She worked down the row with Biscuit supervising from a folding chair. But tucked in the bottom of the last crate, wrapped in a crumpled napkin, was a single white saucer with a gold rim. It had never been washed at all. A thin brown ring of dried tea clung to the center.

Hattie knew that pattern. It matched the monogrammed cup Lionel carried everywhere, the one Colette had unpacked so carefully at the inn. Somebody had cleared the judges' table in a rush and missed it. She did not touch it with her fingers, but lifted it with the napkin and set it gently into an empty cake tin.

Deputy Sam Bramble arrived within the quarter hour. He peered into the tin and let out a low whistle. "Aunt Hattie, the county crew went over this tent twice." "Then they looked at the cups and forgot the saucers," Hattie said. "Nobody ever looks at the saucer." Sam sealed it in an evidence bag, and promised it would go to the state lab in Augusta that very afternoon.

chapters.title: Stick to Pies
chapters.text:
Hattie unlocked the Rolling Pin at five, switched on the ovens, and tied on her flour-dusted smock. Then she saw it: a folded square of paper lying just inside the front door, as if someone had slid it underneath.

Biscuit reached it first and batted it across the tiles. The message was printed in stiff capital letters, the kind a person uses when they do not want their handwriting known. It said: STICK TO PIES, MRS. BRAMBLE. LEAVE THE REST ALONE. There was no name at the bottom, only a smudge of something that might have been ink or might have been soot.

Hattie sat down hard on the stool behind the counter. Her hands were steady, but her heart was thumping like a mixer on high. In thirty years of teaching she had received plenty of anonymous notes, mostly about homework, and not one of them had frightened her. This one came close.

When Winnie came over with the morning cocoa, she read it twice and turned pale. "Hattie, you have to show Sam. Somebody is watching you." "Somebody is worried," Hattie corrected, though she bolted the back door all the same. She slipped the note into a clean bread bag for Sam and copied every word into her green notebook. Then she rolled out the pastry for the apple pies. If someone wanted her to stick to pies, she would make the best pies they had ever tasted, and keep asking questions while they cooled.

chapters.title: Who Knew the Schedule
chapters.text:
On Monday Gordon Pike sent up a cardboard folder from the harbor office with a note that read, For whatever good it does. Inside were the committee papers from the bake-off: entry forms, ribbon orders, and the seating chart for the judges' table. Hattie spread them across her kitchen table while Biscuit sat on the parts she most needed to read.

The public program, the one pinned up all over the village, listed only the categories: breads, pies, preserves, cakes. But at the very back of the folder was a single typed sheet marked PRIVATE, the official judging timetable. It gave every entry a number and an exact time. Entry fourteen, plum cake, Sugar and Spoon, ten forty.

Hattie sat back and frowned. Gordon had penciled a line along the margin: Only three copies printed, one for each judge and their people. Nobody else saw it. That meant the baker herself had not known when her cake would be tasted. The crowd had not known, nor the reporters. Only the judges and the folks who fetched their tea and kept their papers in order.

She thought of Lionel's travel kettle, the honey in his cup, and the long hour before the tasting began. Whoever wanted the blame to fall on Delia would have needed to know precisely when that plum cake reached the table. Hattie underlined the word timetable twice in her green notebook. Biscuit yawned, unimpressed, and shifted onto the seating chart.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't
chapters.text:
Imogen Vale came into the Rolling Pin on Tuesday with blue paint on her cuffs and a lawyer's folder under her arm. She ordered a pumpkin muffin, did not eat it, and finally sat down across from Hattie at the corner table by the window.

"I owe you the truth," Imogen said. "When I told you I would inherit Uncle Lionel's house, I was showing off. The truth is that he never changed his will. He wrote it thirty years ago, and it leaves every penny and every brick to a cooking school scholarship in Portland." She slid the papers across. "His lawyer sent me a copy last spring, because I asked. I already knew I would get nothing but his old easel."

Hattie read the lawyer's letterhead, then looked up. Imogen's eyes were bright, but she held her chin steady. "He used to promise me the house when I was little," she said. "I stopped believing him a long time ago." Hattie reached across and patted her paint-speckled hand.

If Imogen had known since spring that she would inherit nothing, then she had no reason to hurry her uncle along. Hattie wrote it carefully in her green notebook and drew a small box around it. The list of suspects was getting shorter, and the shadows around the ones who remained seemed to grow longer every day. She pushed the pumpkin muffin back toward Imogen and told her to eat something.

chapters.title: Shelves of Seed Catalogs
chapters.text:
Rain drummed on the roof all Wednesday afternoon, so Hattie took a thermos of tea and her notebook to the shared reading room at the Gull's Rest Inn. Dottie Quill had lit a small fire in the grate. The room smelled of old paper, and the lemon oil Dottie rubbed into the shelves every Friday.

The gardening section ran along the whole back wall. There were seed catalogs from the 1950s with hand-tinted pictures of giant tomatoes, a field guide to Maine wildflowers, and a crumbling almanac. Hattie pulled them down one at a time and turned the pages slowly, looking for anything that did not belong.

She learned a good deal more than she expected. Foxglove, one book said, was a handsome biennial that loved cool shade and should never be planted where children or pets might nibble it. Another book had a whole chapter on cottage gardens with a careful drawing of the inn's own walled garden, labeled in faded ink. Biscuit, who had followed her over, curled up on a velvet cushion and snored.

Dottie came by with a plate of shortbread and peered at the stack. "Nobody's touched those in years," she said. Then she paused. "Well, almost nobody. A few of the guests were in here last week, browsing the plant books. I didn't pay much mind to who." Hattie nodded and kept reading, the fire popping softly beside her, until the windows went blue with evening.

chapters.title: A Pressed Leaf
chapters.text:
Hattie came back to the reading room on Thursday morning, determined to finish the gardening shelf. Near the bottom, wedged behind the almanac, she found a slim green volume she had missed the day before: A Practical Guide to Medicinal Plants, printed in Boston in 1931. Its cloth cover was worn soft at the corners, but the spine was not dusty at all. Someone had handled it recently.

She opened it on her lap, and the book fell open by itself. Lying across the page was a single pressed leaf, flat and papery, with a fuzzy underside and toothed edges. Hattie knew it at once. It was a foxglove leaf, carefully dried and slipped between the pages as a bookmark.

The chapter it marked was titled Digitalis and the Heart. Hattie felt a chill. The words described how a few leaves, steeped like tea, could slow a heart until it stopped. There was a small pencil tick in the margin.

She did not pull the leaf free. Instead she slid her own handkerchief beneath the book, closed it gently, and wrapped it in a clean dish towel from her bag. Biscuit watched her from the hearth with round, solemn eyes. Anyone at the inn could have walked into this room and opened this book, and Hattie reminded herself of that firmly. Still, as she walked down the hill toward Sam's office, she could not stop wondering whose patient hands had pressed that leaf, and why.
